# Data preparation

For this analysis, a download script was written in order to obtain latest crime incidence data, it also converts this file to Parquet format to optimize performance.

```{python}
#| eval: false

import polars as pl
import requests
from pathlib import Path

def download_incidence():
    # script folder
    SCRIPT_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
    # script-based routes
    csv_path = SCRIPT_DIR / "data" / "raw_fgj_files.csv"
    parquet_path = SCRIPT_DIR / "data" / "fgj_files.parquet"
    # Create folder
    csv_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    url = "https://tinyurl.com/fgj-files"
    print("Downloading ...")
    res = requests.get(url)
    res.raise_for_status()
    
    with open(csv_path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(res.content)
    
    # save as parquet
    df = pl.read_csv(csv_path, encoding="latin-1")
    df.write_parquet(parquet_path)
    print(f"✅ Processed file saved at: {parquet_path}")

    # remove csv file to keep parquet only
    csv_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)
    print("✅ Removed csv file")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance='simple' icon='false'}
**Manual download**

If you are a `bash` user, you can easily execute this command in your terminal.

```{bash}
curl -L 'https://tinyurl.com/fgj-files' -o fgj_files.csv
```
:::

## Reading the dataset

```{python}
#| label: tbl-incidence-dataset
#| tbl-cap: Incidence dataset preview. <br><br> You can see the table is in wide format, so we will transform it to long format for our analysis.

import polars as pl

data = pl.scan_parquet('data/fgj_files.parquet')
data.head(3).collect().to_pandas().style
```

We create a month mapping to replace month strings by integers.

```{python}
# month mapping
meses_map = {
    'enero': 1,'febrero': 2,'marzo': 3,'abril': 4,'mayo': 5,'junio': 6,'julio': 7,
    'agosto': 8,'septiembre': 9,'octubre': 10,'noviembre': 11,'diciembre': 12
}
```

We do some data transformations to obtain our prepared dataset.

```{python}
df = (
  data
    .unpivot(
      on=['Enero','Febrero','Marzo','Abril','Mayo','Junio',
          'Julio','Agosto','Septiembre','Octubre','Noviembre','Diciembre',
      ],
      index=['Año','Clave_Ent','Entidad','Cve. Municipio','Municipio',
          'Bien jurídico afectado','Tipo de delito','Subtipo de delito','Modalidad',
	    ],
      variable_name='Mes',
      value_name='Incidencia',
      )
    .with_columns(
      pl.col('Mes').str.strip_chars().str.to_lowercase()
    )
    .with_columns(
      pl.col('Mes').replace(meses_map).cast(pl.Int8).alias('Mes_num')
    )
    .with_columns(
      pl.date(pl.col('Año'), pl.col('Mes_num'), 1).alias('Fecha')
    )
    .select([
      'Fecha','Año','Mes','Mes_num','Clave_Ent','Entidad',
      'Cve. Municipio','Municipio','Bien jurídico afectado',
      'Tipo de delito','Subtipo de delito','Modalidad','Incidencia',
    ])
)
```

We check the kinds of robbery included in the dataset in order to filter robbery of pedestrians.

```{python}
(
  df.filter(
    pl.col('Subtipo de delito').str.contains('Robo')
    )
    .collect()
    .get_column('Subtipo de delito')
    .unique()
    .to_list()
)
```

We filter by names provided in the former list to create our data subset of robbery of pedestrians in Mexico City.

```{python}
df_cdmx = (
  df
    .filter(
      (pl.col('Subtipo de delito').str.contains('Robo a transeúnte')),
      (pl.col('Entidad')=='Ciudad de México'),
    )
    .select(
      ['Fecha','Cve. Municipio','Municipio','Subtipo de delito','Modalidad','Incidencia',]
    )
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cdmx-theft
#| tbl-cap: Robbery of Pedestrians Dataset Preview. <br><br> This is the cleaned long-format dataset we will use for our analysis during the period 2015-2025.

(
  df_cdmx
    .collect()
    .sample(5)
    .to_pandas()
    .style
    .format({'Fecha':"{:%Y-%m}"})
    .hide(axis=0)
)
```


# Data analysis

We have selected robbery of pedestrians in Mexico City, because these crimes are highly dependent on urban "hotspots" (metro stations, specific intersections, or commercial corridors), making them perfect for spatial clustering.

## Model implementation

K-Means (Clustering): Best for Robo a Transeúnte (Pedestrian Robbery). It helps you identify "Micro-hotspots." For example, clustering by Latitude/Longitude can reveal that 3 clusters are concentrated around Bellas Artes, Insurgentes, and Polanco.

K-Means for Spatial Hotspots. We will cluster crimes based on their coordinates to find high-incidence zones.

```{python}
#| eval: false

import polars as pl
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
import plotly.express as px

# load dataset
df = pl.read_parquet("data/incidencia_cdmx.parquet")

# 2. Filter for a specific crime (e.g., Pedestrian Robbery)
# Using Polars for high-speed filtering
data_clustering = df.filter(
    pl.col("delito") == "ROBO A TRANSEUNTE EN VIA PUBLICA CON VIOLENCIA"
).select(["latitud", "longitud"]).drop_nulls()

# K-Means
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=10, n_init=10, random_state=42)
clusters = kmeans.fit_predict(data_clustering.to_pandas())

# add clusters back to a DataFrame
data_clustering = data_clustering.with_columns(
    pl.Series(name="cluster", values=clusters).cast(pl.Utf8)
)

# visualization
fig = px.scatter_mapbox(
    data_clustering.to_pandas(), 
    lat="latitud", lon="longitud", 
    color="cluster",
    color_discrete_sequence=["#E3120B", "#005073", "#00AEEF", "#7BA2B3"],
    mapbox_style="carto-positron",
    title="K-Means: Hotspots de Robo a Transeúnte en CDMX"
)

fig.show()
```
